title: Deceased's brother calls for cameras on cruisers
article: Dashboard cameras to record video and audio when police interact with citizens should be installed on OPP cruisers, says the brother of a man who died two years ago in police custody.

David Horan made his submission Tuesday at the inquest examining how his brother, Paul Thomas Horan, 43, died Sept. 24, 2010 in the early morning at Bluewater Health's Charlotte Eleanor Englehart site in Petrolia -- a few hours after his arrest on Highway 402 for failing to stop for police.
Dashboard camera recordings would also protect police officers, Horan said.

After five days of testimony, all the evidence was before the five-member coroner's jury Tuesday afternoon. They will begin deliberations today to determine how Horan died and, possibly, make recommendations to prevent similar deaths.
Final submissions from lawyers representing Bluewater Health, the OPP and doctors suggested Horan's toxic level of antidepressants and methadone was due to suicide.
Suicide can be planned or impulsive, the jurors heard.

Horan, in his testimony, said it's possible his brother panicked when the OPP cruiser's emergency lights went on to pull him over. His brother couldn't handle pressure, Horan said, and perhaps he thought if he popped some pills he would get 72 hours in a mental health ward so he could determine his next move.
The OPP officer who stopped him was taking him to Bluewater Health in Sarnia for a mental health assessment after Horan had said he had a pellet gun in the car so police would be forced to shoot him.
During that trip Horan became unresponsive and the OPP officer called for an ambulance. In the ambulance Horan was convulsing and arrived at the Petrolia hospital in very poor condition.
He'd been prescribed methadone due to a past oxycodone addiction and had also been prescribed an anti-depressant.
A cousin had been speaking with Horan before he headed to his nightshift job in Strathroy and he was in a good mood, jurors heard.
Horan was a decent person and a loving family man, said coroner's counsel Randy Evans during his final submission.

Coroner Dr. Thomas Wilson told jurors they must speak for Paul Horan in their findings, and possible recommendations. He reminded them of the coroner's motto: we speak for the dead to protect the living.
